sections.title: What an eval harness does
paragraphs: An eval harness is a system that runs {{evaluation}}s automatically: pick a dataset, generate {{model}} answers, score them with a {{judge}} or ground-truth labels and report results. Tools like AiEval, LangSmith and PromptLayer are eval harnesses: they wire the generate-score loop so you do not script it by hand.

The core workflow is always the same. Start with a set of {{prompt}}s (test cases). Call one or more {{model}}s to generate answers. Apply a {{rubric}} or reference answers to score quality. Store results for comparison.

Harnesses add convenience: UI for creating evaluations, automation for running many {{model}}s in parallel, dashboards for tracking scores over time and integrations with CI/CD so every code push triggers a regression check.

AiEval is a harness focused on manual and automated {{rubric}}-based scoring. You saw this in the First evaluation lab: create prompt + rubric, run automation, open Compare. That entire flow is the harness at work.
Next: how the pieces connect, from {{prompt}} to {{model}} to {{judge}} to dashboard.
bullets: Eval harness: automates generate → score → report.
Core loop: test {{prompt}}s → {{model}} answers → scoring → results storage.
Convenience: UI, automation, tracking, CI/CD integration.

check.prompt: A teammate suggests: "Let's manually call the {{model}} API, copy-paste answers into a spreadsheet and score by hand." What does a harness provide that this workflow lacks?
check.answer: Automation, tracking over time and reproducibility
choices: Nothing: spreadsheets are just as good.
Automation, tracking over time and reproducibility
The ability to generate answers: APIs cannot do that.
check.explanation: Harnesses automate repetitive steps, log results for comparison across {{model}} versions and ensure the same test runs the same way every time.

sections.title: Generate, score, improve: the feedback loop
paragraphs: Evaluation is not a one-time task. Production teams run evaluations weekly, daily or on every code change to catch regressions. The harness makes this repeatable: same {{prompt}}s, same {{rubric}}, new {{model}} or new prompt wording.

The cycle: generate answers with your current {{model}} or prompt and score them. If quality is below your bar, adjust. Try a different {{model}}, rewrite the {{prompt}} or refine the {{rubric}}. Then re-run and compare scores.
Click each step below to see how the loop fits together. Improvement is iterative: no one ships a perfect system on the first try.
Harnesses track history, so you can see: "We switched from Model A to Model B and accuracy went from 75% to 82%." That data justifies {{model}} upgrades and catches when updates make things worse.

reveals.reveal: Call the {{model}} API with your test {{prompt}}s. Store each answer alongside the prompt for scoring.
Apply the {{rubric}} (either via human review or a {{judge}} {{model}}). Record scores per {{criterion}}.
Look at the results. If quality is low, identify which {{criterion}} failed. Adjust {{model}}, {{prompt}} or {{rubric}}.
Generate and score again with the changes. Compare new scores to the baseline. Ship if improved, iterate if not.

check.prompt: Your harness shows that accuracy dropped from 85% to 78% after a {{model}} update. What is the next step?
check.answer: Inspect failing test cases to understand what changed
choices: Ship anyway: the model vendor knows best.
Inspect failing test cases to understand what changed
Assume the harness is broken and ignore the result.
check.explanation: Scores are signals, not dictates. Inspect what failed, decide if the regression matters for your use case, then revert or adjust accordingly.

sections.title: Building your own or using a tool
paragraphs: Small teams often start by scripting evals: a Python loop that calls {{model}} APIs, a CSV of test cases, manual scoring in a spreadsheet. That works for dozens of tests but breaks at hundreds.

Off-the-shelf harnesses (AiEval, LangSmith, Braintrust, PromptLayer) save time. They handle API retries, parallel execution, result storage and dashboards. The trade-off is learning a new tool and accepting its workflow.

If your needs are unique (custom scoring logic, proprietary {{model}}s, integration with internal CI), building a harness is justified. Use a task queue (Celery, BullMQ), a database for results (Postgres, SQLite) and a dashboard (Streamlit, React).
Either way, the principles stay the same: reproducible test cases, automated scoring, tracked history. Whether you build or buy, the goal is to make evaluation cheap enough to run often.

You have now completed the core curriculum. You understand {{supervisedLearning}}, {{prompt}} design, {{rubric}}s, {{judge}}s and how harnesses connect the pieces. Next: apply this to your own evaluations.
bullets: Script vs tool: DIY for unique needs, off-the-shelf for speed.
Core needs: test cases, automation, storage, dashboards.
Goal: make evaluation cheap and repeatable.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what does an eval harness automate?
check.explanation: A harness automates the repetitive steps: calling {{model}}s, scoring answers, storing results and comparing over time.
